title: Deepak Ranganatha Sastry Mamillapalli
OCR tool to find cartridges on a shelf
text:
Job search after graduating from grad school hasn’t exactly gone swimmingly. I took up a part time retail job to keep the bills paid while I continued looking for jobs. I am not sure I can mention the name of the company here but it’s a company that sells stationery and rhymes with “maples”.
Anyway, part of my job included stocking the shelves. Basically, if something isn’t on display and we had the stock, I had to move it from the storage to the display.
For most categories, this was fine; the search itself didn’t take very long because I knew where most of the stock used to be. For printer ink cartridges however, this proved to be very annoying.
The problem was that there were too many types of cartridges. HP alone has released well over 100 different cartridge model numbers. What’s worse is that neither the display nor the storage was sorted by any key (neither the model number nor the SKU/UPC). So if there was a gap in display, I had to scan the 100s of boxes we had in the storage looking for the exact one. What adds to the complexity is that cartridges can also be of multiple types: standard or XL cartridges which had more ink.
For HP cartridges alone, the overhead storage spanned three different sections. So I would need to wheel the ladder to the first section, manually check each row to see if the cartridge I had was there and then move the ladder over to the next if it wasn’t and resume searching. This was annoying as often times I’d miss the cartridge and I would have to wheel back the ladder to a previous section to grab it.
I thought this problem was easily solvable with some optical recognition model which is exactly what I built. I used PaddleOCR that took in a photo and return a list of every string it found with a bounding box and a confidence score. The matching takes that list and decides whether the cartridge number I was looking for exists or not. If it does, it annotates the image and sends it back. At work, I just take a photo and input the list of boxes and the type of cartridge I am looking for, and get back the annotated image. I used FastAPI on the serving path and password protected it with a signed-cookie. Frontend is just a basic HTML file. I self-hosted it using a CloudFlare tunnel because I didn’t want to pay to host it on an EC2 instance.



An image of the topstock/overhead storage.

title: Projects
text:
M.Sc. thesis. Intelligent Robot Learning Lab, University of Alberta, with PCL Construction. April 2025 – June 2026.
Construction planners decide what order to build things in. On a huge construction site (like commercial buildings), the order matters more than it sounds. Crews that jump across the construction site lose a lot of time in demobilizing and moving. A plan that needs forty workers one week and ten the next is expensive as it adds a lot of overhead costs and is also hard to staff. Planners do this by hand and are good at this but they are balancing multiple objectives (often conflicting) at the same time.
Furthermore, sequences had to follow certain constraints. On a job site, there could be precedence constraints (e.g I have to finish laying concrete before I work on wiring) as well as physical constraints (e.g I can’t violate the laws of gravity; I can’t build in the air without having support below).
I worked on turning this into a problem RL can solve. I framed construction scheduling as a MDP where the reward function accounts for crew movement, labour curve smoothing and duration of the project. The RL agent coordinates multiple disciplines (or trades) across a construction site minimizing these costs. To incorporate these constraints, I used action masking which got rid of the invalid actions at each time step, ensuring that the final sequence is a valid one.
To find out if any of this mattered, I ran a human study against professional planners who worked with the industry partner for this project (PCL Construction) on a subarea of a real construction project. The agent’s labour curves came out about 60% smoother, with total duration within 6-10% of the strongest baseline and shorter than the schedules designed by humans.
Although this was a proof of concept, there is a lot more work to be done. I wanted to explore the use of search and RL; since the model of the environment can pretty easily be learned maybe pure RL isn’t the best choice. When I write this into a journal, I’ll look into alternative formulations.



Intelligent Robot Learning Lab, University of Alberta. June 2023 – January 2024.
I worked on optimizing FPGA placements using RL.
A FPGA is a chip you can configure after manufacturing, as opposed to ASIC chips (which, as the name suggests, are specific to the application and aren’t usually configurable). Placement decides which physical location each block sits in on the chip. This choice determines how much wire is needed to connect all the blocks, and this in turn determines how fast the chip can run.
Placement optimization is a widely studied problem in chip design. There are many traditional methods that solve this. For example, Simulated Annealing is widely used for this: propose a swap, keep if it helps, reject if it doesn’t, and every now and then accept a bad swap. It works extremely well and has been the go-to for many decades.
We wanted to find out if RL could learn to place blocks directly. The state space was just the image of the chip board at the current state and an embedding generated by a GNN to process the netlist (i.e what blocks are connected). The action was choosing a location for each block and the reward was the final wirelength which could only be calculated after all the blocks were placed, making this a sparse reward setting.
Since it was a hard RL problem (the state space was ginormous), the agent was getting stuck at suboptimal placements. In order to encourage it to explore more, we added Random Network Distillation and that helped a bit.
Furthermore, instead of placing every block in one go, we split the board into subproblems and let an agent solve each one. This improved the performance quite a bit.
See Publications for the ISEDA 2024 and NeurIPS 2023 workshop papers.

title: Projects
text:
Personal

Cartridge Finder
I built an app that helps me find cartridges on shelves. Basically, I take a photograph from my phone, type the cartridge number I want and I get an annotated pic back with the matches.
It runs on my local machine, reachable from a browser over a Cloudflare tunnel with password protection. The OCR model sits behind a single interface, so swapping it means changing one file rather than touching the matching or serving code.
I hand-labeled an eval set containing 456 boxes and wrote a scoring script. It finds 97% of the queried cartridges, and 9% of the boxes it draws are wrong.
Code: https://github.com/DeepakR-Sastry/cartridge_detection Blogpost (coming soon): https://deepakr-sastry.github.io/blog/posts/cartridge-finder.html
